newsitem.title: BRAZIL: BRAZIL CONGRESS WEEK-Reforms on the agenda, again.
newsitem.headline: BRAZIL CONGRESS WEEK-Reforms on the agenda, again.

text.p: The saga of Brazil's CIVIL SERVICE REFORM was due to run on this week as the government prepared, yet again, to hold a vote on a key amendment to the bill in the Chamber of Deputies.

For more than two months, government whips have been delaying a vote on the amendment, which would maintain lifetime job guarantees for civil servants, fearing they would not muster the three-fifths majority needed to kill it.

"We want to hold the vote this week, but we'll have to see what the leaders of the political parties have to say when they arrive in Brasilia Tuesday," said an aide to deputy Luis Eduardo Magalhaes, the government's leader in the lower house.
Failure to defeat the amendment would leave the already diluted reform as toothless as the PENSION REFORM BILL when it was stripped of its main points in the Chamber of Deputies last year.
A rewritten version of the pension bill may be put to a vote in a Senate committee Tuesday. Amendments to the bill would then be voted next week.
Both bills were sent to Congress two years ago, but have been bogged down by stiff resistance from lawmakers and a powerful public sector lobby opposed to the end of perks for civil servants.
Lawmakers have conceded the reforms might have to wait until after next year's presidential, congressional and state governorship elections which are already starting to dominate the political scene.
Government whips were expected to announce this week whether they will call an EXTRAORDINARY SESSION of Congress to run through the July recess in a bid to make up for lost time.

Another important piece of legislation facing a vote in the Chamber of Deputies this week was the government's GENERAL TELECOMMUNICATIONS LAW, a bill which would regulate the privatization of Brazil's giant telecommunications sector.
An aide to Deputy Alberto Goldman, who drew up the bill, said the vote might take place Wednesday followed by votes on more than 80 amendments next week.

A bill to extend the government's FISCAL STABILIZATION FUND until 1999 might also be voted this week in a lower house committee. The government uses to the fund to keep about $22 billion of tax receipts earmarked by the constitution for states and municipalities, enabling it to balance the federal budget.

A current version of the fund expires June 30, but lawmakers say subsequent approval of the bill to extend it will be retroactive to that date. As a constitutional amendment, it requires two three-fifths majorities in each house of Congress.
Despite the relatively heavy schedule of voting, lawmakers may yet be distracted by ongoing hearings into two alleged CORRUPTION SCANDALS.

Communications Minister Sergio Motta was due to give testimony Tuesday to a lower house panel on an alleged CASH-FOR-VOTES scandal involving a bill that allows President Fernando Henrique Cardoso to run for re-election.

In the Senate, also Tuesday, Sao Paulo governor Mario Covas was scheduled to address a committee trying to trace hundreds of millions of dollars thought to have been siphoned off from underpriced MUNICIPAL AND STATE BONDS trading.
